pages.text: Food and Digestion

image.note: Cover: a plate of food and a winding path through the body

pages.text: Contents. The Journey Begins / The Mouth and the Long Tube / The Stomach / The Small Intestine / The End of the Journey / Looking After Your Gut.

Think of your last meal. Right now, deep inside you, it is on an extraordinary journey: a journey of nearly nine metres, lasting almost a whole day, that turns a plate of food into the living, running, thinking you. This is the story of digestion, the slow and secret unmaking of your dinner.

image.note: A meal with a winding path traced through the body

pages.text: Your body cannot use food as it is. A mouthful of rice, a bite of chicken, a piece of mango: these are far too big and too whole for your tiny body parts to use. So your body takes each meal to pieces, smaller and smaller, until it is small enough to slip into your blood and become part of you. Let us follow a single meal, all the way through.

image.note: Whole food breaking into ever-smaller pieces

pages.text: The journey of your food is really a journey down one long, winding tube that runs right through you, from your mouth at the top to the very bottom. It is coiled and folded to fit, but if you could stretch it out straight, it would be longer than a bus. Your food travels the whole length of it, changed at every stage.

image.note: The digestive tube, coiled then shown stretched out

pages.text: At each stop along this tube, the body does something different to the food: crushes it, soaks it, churns it, and finally soaks up the goodness. It is a kind of factory line, and it never shuts down. Even as you read this, a meal from hours ago is somewhere along the line, being taken quietly to pieces.

image.note: A factory line of digestion stages

chapters.title: The Mouth and the Long Tube

pages.text: It begins in your mouth, with your teeth. Your front teeth cut, your back teeth grind, and together they crush your food into a soft, wet lump. Meanwhile your mouth waters, on purpose, for saliva is not just water. It carries special juices that begin, even now, to break the food down.

image.note: Teeth crushing food, saliva mixing in

pages.text: When the lump is ready, your tongue pushes it to the back of your throat, and you swallow. Now the food enters a tube called the oesophagus, which carries it down to your stomach. And here is a surprise: the food does not simply fall. The tube squeezes it along, in waves, pushing it down whether you are sitting, standing, or upside down.

image.note: The oesophagus squeezing food down in waves

pages.text: This squeezing is so strong that you could, in truth, swallow a mouthful while hanging upside down, and it would still travel the right way, up to your stomach, against gravity. Your food does not fall through you. It is carried, pushed along by muscle, every centimetre of the way.

image.note: A person upside down, food still travelling correctly

pages.text: The oesophagus leads to the stomach, a stretchy bag of muscle that is your food's next great test. Here the food is churned and squeezed and mixed, like clothes in a washing machine, into a thick soup. And mixed in with it is something powerful indeed: acid.

image.note: The stomach churning food into a soup

pages.text: Your stomach makes an acid strong enough to dissolve tough food, and even to kill most of the germs that ride in on it. It is so strong it could burn your skin, and yet it does not burn your stomach, for your stomach protects itself with a thick coat of slime, made fresh every day.

image.note: Stomach acid at work, protected by its lining

pages.text: For a few hours the stomach churns away, until your meal is a smooth, sour soup, ready for the next and most important stage of all. Then, a little at a time, it lets the soup through into the next part of the tube, and the real work of feeding your body begins.

image.note: The stomach releasing soupy food onward

pages.text: Now the food enters the small intestine, a long, coiled tube where the true magic of digestion happens. Here the food is broken into its very smallest pieces, and here, at last, the goodness is taken out of it and passed into your blood, to be carried to every hungry corner of your body.

image.note: The coiled small intestine, goodness passing to blood

pages.text: The walls of this tube are not smooth. They are covered in millions of tiny finger-like bumps, which are covered in even tinier bumps, all to make the inside surface enormous. Spread flat, the lining of your small intestine would cover a whole tennis court, all folded up inside your belly to soak up as much goodness as it can.

image.note: Tiny finger-like bumps lining the intestine

pages.text: Through these millions of bumps, the goodness from your food, the parts that build muscle, feed your brain, and give you energy, slips into your blood and is whisked away. This is the moment your dinner truly becomes you. The rice you ate becomes the legs that run and the fingers that turn this page.

image.note: Nutrients passing into the blood, carried through the body

pages.text: By now, nearly all the goodness has been taken out, and what is left is mostly waste and water. This passes into the last part of the tube, the large intestine, whose main job is to soak up the water your body wants to keep, so none is wasted.

image.note: The large intestine soaking up water

pages.text: What remains after that, the parts your body truly cannot use, is stored, and later passed out of the body when you go to the toilet. It is a natural and necessary end to the journey, the tidy finish of a meal that began, nearly a day before, on your plate.

image.note: The final, dry waste ready to leave the body

pages.text: So a single meal takes almost a whole day to travel through you, crushed, soaked, churned, and soaked up, nine metres of winding tube from start to finish. And by the end, the parts your body needed are already at work inside you, and the rest is quietly gone.

image.note: The complete journey of a meal, start to finish

pages.text: Your digestive system works best when you help it. Chew your food well, and you do half its work for it. Drink plenty of water, for the whole journey needs it. And eat foods with plenty of fibre, the rough parts of fruit, vegetables, and grains, which sweep through the tube and keep it all moving smoothly.

image.note: Healthy foods: fruit, vegetables, grains, water

pages.text: Deep in your gut live trillions of tiny helpers, friendly germs that help break your food down and keep you well. You cannot see them, but they are on your side, and a healthy, varied diet keeps them happy. Look after them, and they will look after you.

image.note: Friendly gut helpers pictured, working in the intestine

pages.text: Words to know. Saliva: the juice in your mouth that starts digestion. Oesophagus: the tube from mouth to stomach. Stomach: the muscly bag that churns food with acid. Small intestine: where goodness passes into the blood. Fibre: the rough part of food that keeps things moving.

image.note: Labelled diagram of the digestive system

pages.text: Your food becomes your blood, your muscles, your very thoughts, all through this quiet, winding journey inside you. Every meal you eat is being turned, right now, into more of you. What will you feed your amazing body next?

image.note: A meal transforming into a running, thinking child
